title: Hallelujah Chorus
description: Handel's Hallelujah chorus from Messiah, for 4 singers, in his own four voice parts and his key, D, as Ebenezer Prout's 1902 edition prints them, without the orchestra. Sung whole: the Hallelujahs, the quiet "The kingdom of this world", the voices coming in one by one on "And He shall reign", and the sopranos' long notes climbing through "King of Kings" to a top A.

credits.words: Charles Jennens's words for Messiah, from Revelation 19:6, 11:15 and 19:16 (King James Version)
credits.arrangement: Handel's own four voice parts (Prout's edition, 1902), adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: Charles Jennens, who wrote the words of Messiah (Dictionary of National Biography, 1885 to 1900, "Jennens, Charles", by Gordon Goodwin: "He also wrote the words for Handel's 'Saul' (1735), 'Messiah' (1742)"; "died unmarried on 20 Nov. 1773"), set from Revelation 19:6, 11:15 and 19:16 in the King James Version (1611), in Jennens's wording as Prout's edition prints it; in the UK the King James Version is under Crown letters patent (a question with our lawyer, as for The Lord Bless You)
licence.tune: public domain: Handel died 1759; the title page of Prout's edition says Messiah was "composed in the year 1741"
licence.arrangement: Handel's own four voice parts as Ebenezer Prout's edition prints them (Novello, 1902; Prout died 1909; public domain), every pitch and word as printed but for the changes named here, sung without the orchestra: the three bars of orchestral introduction are left out, so the song starts at the choir's first "Hallelujah" (bar 4), and every bar the choir sings is kept, its two short rests for all four parts too (three beats before "The kingdom of this world", two before the last "Hallelujah"). In Handel's key, D, as choirs sing it; tempo 60 (Prout prints crotchet = 72), the fastest at which Handel's quaver rests are a breath and his semiquaver "Hal-le" a quarter of a second. Prout's restored underlay is kept: "jah, Hal-" on one note in the alto (bar 24), soprano (bar 30) and bass (bars 31 and 32), and the tenor's "and He shall reign, and He shall reign" (bars 70 and 71). At bars 46 and 79 Prout prints a small lower D under the alto's top D; the alto sings the top note. Breaths written in for beginners, each taken from the end of a line's last note: before "reigneth" in each "for the Lord God Omnipotent reigneth"; after "become" and "Lord" and at the comma after the first "Christ" of "is become the Kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and of His Christ;" in every part; before "for" in each "and He shall reign for ever and ever"; before each "King of Kings" that follows "ever"; and the long "Kings" and "Lords" held a beat to four beats less (no line over 9 seconds), "world" (bar 35) a beat less in every part. The tenor's "for" at bars 25 and 29 starts half a beat late, after a breath (Handel's "Hallelujah!" runs into it on a quaver). Accepted exceptions (singable.py), all Handel's own writing in his key: rule 4, every note outside the beginner ranges: the soprano's F-sharp 5 (bars 8 to 11, 15, 16, 22, 23, 29, 37, 49, 63, 64, 66, 68, 75 to 79, 86 and 87), G5 (bars 23, 66 to 68, 75 to 78 and 87) and A5 ("He", bar 49), with its held F-sharp and G on the climbing "King of Kings" and "Lord of Lords" (bars 63 to 68) at the top of the range; the alto's D5 ("He", bars 46 and 79, where Prout prints a small lower D as an option); the tenor's F-sharp 4 and G4 in most Hallelujahs, in "for the Lord God Omnipotent" and in "King of Kings" (bars 4 to 92) and its A4 ("lu-" bar 24, "He" bar 44); the bass's B3, C-sharp 4 and D4 in most Hallelujahs and in "for the Lord God Omnipotent", "King of Kings" and "and He shall reign" (bars 8 to 86); so the soprano's, tenor's and bass's middles sit above the middle of their beginner ranges; rule 5, the alto's, tenor's and bass's slurs (Handel's melismas on "Hal-le", "be-come", "our", "ev-er" and "reign"), the octave leaps of "God Om-ni-po-tent" in every part and the leaps of the subject of "And He shall reign"; rule C, the parallel octaves and doubled leading notes of Handel's unison and octave passages ("for the Lord God Omnipotent reigneth", bars 12 to 14, 17 to 19, 25 to 27 and 29 to 31), the tenor above the alto in bars 28, 31, 38 and 50 and the bass above the tenor in bars 14 and 68.

Handel, "edited, and the additional accompaniments largely re-written, by Ebenezer Prout" (London: Novello and Company, Limited; New York: Novello, Ewer and Co.; "Copyright, 1902, by Novello and Company, Limited"; plate 11570), full score, No. 44, Chorus, Hallelujah, pp. 260 to 278, Allegro, crotchet = 72, in D, sung here in that key; read from the University of Toronto, Faculty of Music copy at archive.org/details/messiahsacredora00hand_0 (page images n285 to n303; Prout's preface on No. 44, p. xv, at n20), with every bar compared with Prout's vocal score of the same edition (Novello's Original Octavo Edition, "edited, and the pianoforte accompaniment largely re-written, by Ebenezer Prout", "Copyright, 1902"; a later, undated printing naming the H. W. Gray Co. as New York agents), No. 44, pp. 149 to 157, archive.org/details/bwb_KT-315-920 (n162 to n170): the voice parts and words agree note for note
